text: The asphalt paving up to the Mapleton gates
why: ¶124 states the tracks end at the asphalt paving leading up to the Mapleton stable gates.

text: The gates of the Mapleton stables
why: ¶124 names the gates of the Mapleton stables as where the tracks end.
¶124 says a groom ran out from the Mapleton stables as they approached.

text: Thursday evening, at the gates of the Mapleton stables
why: Breakfast was Thursday morning (¶13), and ¶113 has the sun setting during the walk, placing the arrival at the gates in the evening.

text: When the same tracks came back to the Mapleton gates
why: ¶122-124 state that the tracks come back in the opposite direction and end at the Mapleton gates.

text: Did Silas Brown and the Mapleton people have a hand in the affair? — he found the horse loose and took it in
id: q.brown_part=he found the horse loose and took it in
why: The question of Mapleton involvement is fair (¶66-67 raise Brown's bets and his hostility to Straker), but the answer 'he found the horse loose and took it in' is a specific mechanism the story has not suggested, and it presumes the Mapleton people hold the horse.

text: Who was the man whose track joined the horse's near Mapleton? — someone from the Mapleton stables
why: The man's track joins the horse's and leads to the Mapleton gates, where a groom appears, so a Mapleton man is a possibility the story gives reason to consider.
